## Q&A {.scrollable .smaller}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Q: Why was there a problem with the police not knowing whether the participants ingested a placebo, lower percentage, or higher percentage of THC?"}
A: I was not as clear as I should have been in this! The police knew that some participants received a placebo and some did not (that's fine!), but they *also* knew how long it had been since they had smoked the joint. So, they would have expected (given knowing this information) that at each subsequent field sobriety test that they should maybe expect fewer and fewer participants to be impaired. Given unlimited resources, a more ideal design would have been to bring officers in randomly, without them knowing how far along the study was, so they didn't have any expectation/knowledge about how recently someone could have smoked (which is the case at the roadside...they don't know)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Q: confused about the cutoffs - what do they mean"}
A: The cutoffs are *if* we used that cutoff to determine someone had recently used then how many people would be "over the limit." 
:::

# Principles for effective visualizations {background-color="#92A86A"}

## Principles for effective visualizations

-   Order matters
-   Put long categories on the y-axis
-   Keep scales consistent
-   Select meaningful colors
-   Use meaningful and nonredundant labels

## Data

In September 2019, YouGov survey asked 1,639 GB adults the following question:

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
> In hindsight, do you think Britain was right/wrong to vote to leave EU?
>
> -   Right to leave\
> -   Wrong to leave\
> -   Don't know
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.cell}

:::

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::

:::
:::

::: aside
Source: [YouGov Survey Results](https://d25d2506sfb94s.cloudfront.net/cumulus_uploads/document/x0msmggx08/YouGov%20-%20Brexit%20and%202019%20election.pdf), retrieved Oct 7, 2019
:::

## The Data: Code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brexit <- tibble(
  opinion = c(
    rep("Right", 664), rep("Wrong", 787), rep("Don't know", 188)
  ),
  region = c(
    rep("london", 63), rep("rest_of_south", 241), rep("midlands_wales", 145), rep("north", 176), rep("scot", 39),
    rep("london", 110), rep("rest_of_south", 257), rep("midlands_wales", 152), rep("north", 176), rep("scot", 92),
    rep("london", 24), rep("rest_of_south", 49), rep("midlands_wales", 57), rep("north", 48), rep("scot", 10)
  )
)
```
:::


## Order matters

**Alphabetical is rarely ideal**

::: panel-tabset
### Plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=2100}
:::
:::


### Code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(brexit, aes(x = opinion)) +
  geom_bar()
```

:::

::: {.cell}


## Use inherent level order

::: panel-tabset
### Relevel

`fct_relevel`: Reorder factor levels using a custom order


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="3-6"}
brexit <- brexit |>
  mutate(
    region = fct_relevel( 
      region,
      "london", "rest_of_south", "midlands_wales", "north", "scot"
    )
  )
```
:::


### Plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

:::
:::

:::

`fct_recode`: Change factor levels by hand


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="3-10"}

    region = fct_recode(

      `Rest of South` = "rest_of_south",

      North = "north",
      Scotland = "scot"
```

# Pick a purpose {background-color="#92A86A"}

## Segmented bar plots can be hard to read

::: panel-tabset
### Plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=2100}
:::
:::


### Code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="1"}
ggplot(brexit, aes(y = region, fill = opinion)) + 
  geom_bar()
```
:::

:::

## Use facets

::: panel-tabset
### Plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=90%}
:::
:::


### Code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="3"}
ggplot(brexit, aes(y = opinion, fill = region)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~region, nrow = 1) 
```
:::

:::

## Keep scales consistent

::: panel-tabset
### Plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=90%}
:::
:::


### Code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="3"}
ggplot(brexit, aes(y = opinion)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~region, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x")
```
:::

:::

-   `scales = "free_x"` gives each panel its own x-axis: Scotland's "Wrong" bar (92 people) now looks as long as Rest of South's (257)
-   The default (fixed scales) keeps panels comparable; only free scales on purpose, and say so

## Manually choose colors when needed

### Code

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="9-13"}
ggplot(brexit, aes(y = opinion, fill = opinion)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~region, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 12)) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(title = "Was Britain right/wrong to vote to leave EU?",
       subtitle = "YouGov Survey Results, 2-3 September 2019",
       caption = "Source: bit.ly/2lCJZVg",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c( 
    "Wrong" = "red", 
    "Right" = "green", 
    "Don't know" = "gray" 
  )) 
```
:::

:::

. . .

But: red-green is the most common form of color vision deficiency (roughly 1 in 12 men), so these two bars can look nearly identical to many viewers.

## Principles recap {.smaller}

What we covered (cite these by name in your homework and case studies):

-   **Keep it simple**: skip 3D and pies when a bar chart does the job
-   **Use color to draw attention** to what matters
-   **Tell a story**: annotate the takeaway
-   **Order matters**: avoid alphabetical; order by frequency or inherent order
-   **Put long categories on the y-axis**
-   **Keep scales consistent** across panels
-   **Pick a purpose**: decide which comparison the plot should make easy (e.g., facets vs. stacked bars)
-   **Select meaningful colors**: colorblind-friendly, consistent meaning
-   **Use meaningful and nonredundant labels**: titles, subtitles, sources
